hints: Each coin can be used once, but the jar may hold two coins of value 1. What goes wrong if you treat them as different coins?

Sort the coins, backtrack with a start index, and move to j+1 after using coins[j]. At the same depth, skip a value equal to the previous one (j > start && coins[j] == coins[j-1]) so the same multiset is never built twice.

1. Sort coins.
  2. go(start, left): if left == 0, save a copy.
  3. Loop j from start; if coins[j] > left, break.
  4. If j > start and coins[j] == coins[j-1], continue.
  5. Add coins[j], call go(j+1, left - coins[j]), remove it.

approaches.name: Brute force + set
approaches.idea: Try all 2<sup>n</sup> subsets of coins, keep those summing to target, and dedupe sorted lists with a set.

approaches.name: Optimal: sorted backtracking with duplicate skip
approaches.idea: Sort, use each index once, skip equal values at the same depth and break when a coin is too big.
approaches.time: O(2<sup>n</sup> · n) worst case, heavily pruned by the target

explain: With [4,1,2,4,3,1] sorted to [1,1,2,3,4,4] and target = 6: starting with the first 1 we find 1,1,4 and 1,2,3; the second 1 at the top level is skipped because it equals the first. Starting at 2 we find 2,4 once (the second 4 is skipped at that depth). Starting at 3 or 4 nothing works. The result is 3 combos with no repeats. Sorting also lets us break as soon as a coin exceeds the amount left.
recognize: 'Each coin used at most once' + 'values may repeat' + 'no duplicate combos' → sort, recurse at j+1, skip equal values at the same depth.
